summary: Observation of the movement of a luminous orange ball: probably a Thai lantern.
description: The witness observed, in the southern-southeast suburbs of Paris, a luminous orange orb flying at low altitude towards the city. The description and movement, influenced by the southerly wind (see weather report), perfectly match the appearance of a Thai lantern. This festive period is conducive to licking these lanterns. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable Thai lantern.

summary: Observation of the movement of an orange luminous phenomenon: probable Thai lantern.
description: The witness observed for one or two minutes an orange light moving from east to north at approximately 45° elevation (see simulation on a sky chart, based on the witness's account) at a steady speed, and then it suddenly disappeared. A police report was sent to us in March 2012. The described characteristics are consistent with those of a Thai lantern; the day's weather forecast indicated a light, unstable wind, blowing from south to north at 8 PM and 10 PM (but from north to south at 9 PM!), which could explain the movement in that direction, but without certainty. Given the holiday season, a lantern release this evening is not surprising. This is the hypothesis that GEIPAN (the French National Astronomical Investigation Group) is considering: this case is classified as "B": probable Thai lantern.

summary: Observation of the movement of orange luminous phenomena: probable Thai lanterns.
description: On December 25, 2011, between 6:35 PM and 6:40 PM, a driver and passenger observed a bright, stationary light in the sky, moving in a pendulum-like motion. Initially thinking it was fireworks, the witness continued driving and then stopped to take photographs. Upon arriving home, he observed three colored luminous masses following one another in a line as they rose in altitude. The objects disappeared very quickly. No noise was heard during the observation, which lasted several minutes. The police received no other reports of this phenomenon. The Thai lantern hypothesis remains the most likely explanation, consistent with the wind and the photographs, and highly plausible given the date of the observation. However, the irregular movement of the lanterns raises questions: the possibility of updrafts along their path should be considered. This case is classified as Class B, indicating a probable observation of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observations of the atmospheric reentry of the 4th stage of the Soyuz-FG launcher.
description: GEIPAN received several email reports of spectacular luminous trails in the sky on the afternoon of December 24, 2011. In addition, four observations made by airplane pilots were reported to GEIPAN: all described a strong luminous phenomenon observed at very high altitude above the Strasbourg-Black Forest region. The official American website for information on space debris re-entry, reentrynews.aero, indicates that the object numbered 2011 078B re-entered the atmosphere at 4:26 PM UTC, therefore at the same time as the observations. The last recorded orbit closely crossed the observation sites. The debris in question has been identified as the fourth stage of the Soyuz-FG rocket launched on December 21, 2011, at 13:16 UTC from the Baekonour Cosmodrome, for mission TMA-03M: sending three cosmonauts to the ISS. All witnesses clearly observed the reentry of the fourth stage of the Soyuz-FG rocket launched on December 21, 2011.

summary: Observation of the rectilinear and silent movement of a red object with two or three yellow lights in its center: probable observation of the passage of a Thai lantern.
description: On December 20, 2011, at approximately 10:05 PM, a witness observed a red object with lights in its center moving silently in a straight line across the sky. This observation describes the characteristics of Thai lanterns: red-orange orbs moving with the wind (west wind, see weather report). The end-of-year holiday season may have been the reason for this modest lantern release. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable observation of a Thai lantern.

summary: Observation of the presence in the sky of powerful fires appearing to originate from a triangular shape: lack of information.
description: On December 10, 2011, at 4:10 PM, a motorist on the A16 motorway, traveling from Paris near Froissy, observed "numerous very bright lights above the horizon" in the stormy sky. These lights appeared to originate from a triangular shape rising rapidly into the dark clouds before reappearing and then quickly disappearing due north. According to the witness, several other vehicles slowed down during the observation. However, GEIPAN (the French UFO research group) received no other reports. Given the moderate strangeness and limited consistency of the current evidence (only one witness, uncertain location and viewing direction), the hypotheses considered (space debris reentry, Thales lanterns) are not sufficiently consistent with the observation report to be considered. Pending further reports, this case is classified as C due to a lack of information.

summary: Observation of the movement of two yellow lights with a change of direction: lack of information.
description: A witness reported observations made on December 10, 2011, around 8:30 p.m. from their home (see the investigation report). This phenomenon is ultimately not very strange due to the speed and fairly common movement of these luminous points. The hypothesis of foreign military aircraft flying over the area without contact or radar transponder remains the most plausible, but GEIPAN cannot substantiate it due to a lack of radar information. Therefore, this case remains classified as Class C for the time being due to a lack of evidence.

summary: Observation of silent evolutions in the sky reveals a luminous phenomenon of ovoid shape and orange color: lack of cross-checks.
description: On December 2, 2011, between 9:15 and 9:30 PM, a witness at their window observed a luminous phenomenon in the Parisian sky. A bright point moved rapidly along a straight trajectory. After 5 to 6 seconds, this point ignited, and the witness saw an ovoid, orange object appear. No trail or halo was observed. The object then began to rotate, hovered, and then zigzagged after three rotations before moving off again at slow speed. Unfortunately, it was hidden by a building. No unusual noise was heard. The observation lasted approximately 20 seconds. Only one witness account was recorded. This observation began like a typical atmospheric reentry of a meteoroid (fireball), but ended in a completely unusual spiral, a scenario entirely impossible for a celestial body. At this time of day, at this time of year, very few satellites are visible. The first part of the observation could correspond to the observation of a satellite directly reflecting sunlight temporarily (flare), but the end of the observation does not fit this hypothesis at all. It is also possible that these are two independent phenomena, but again, luminous objects moving in a spiral are extremely rare, especially at this speed. Given the unique nature of the witness in a highly urbanized area, the consistency of this case is insufficient to characterize such an unusual phenomenon. GEIPAN classifies this case as "C" due to a lack of corroborating evidence.

summary: Observations by several witnesses of a stationary phenomenon in the sky, bright and white. No sound heard.
description: On November 27, 2011, at 6:50 PM, a driver and her children were intrigued by the presence of a stationary luminous phenomenon above the church in the village of Saint-Gatien-des-Bois (Calvados, Lower Normandy region). A fifth witness later came forward with their testimony. The four witnesses, all from the same family, observed and described the same UFO, and their accounts were consistent. Their testimony was corroborated by a fifth witness, a 10-year-old boy who also observed the UFO, making this a very consistent case. The reality of the phenomenon is beyond doubt. It should be noted, however, that the observation was brief for T1 to T4 (approximately 2 minutes), and even very brief for T5 (a few seconds). The strangeness of the case is more difficult to define: indeed, the materiality of the phenomenon is not confirmed. The initial statements from witnesses describe an object with headlights, but upon reflection, the witnesses are no longer certain they actually saw the object, only the headlights. Now, if this phenomenon is only luminous, it is not very strange; if it is material, it becomes truly so. As it remains unexplained despite a thorough investigation, GEIPAN classifies this case as D. As a consistent but moderately strange case, since it is probably not material, this case is classified as D1.

summary: Observation of an atmospheric reentry of a bolide.
description: On November 26, 2011, at 4:53 a.m., a witness observed a bright point of light with a green trail. The witness's description perfectly matches that of a fireball: a bright light with a green trail, a straight trajectory, and a duration of a few seconds. A fireball is the phenomenon produced by the entry into the upper atmosphere of a large meteorite (weighing more than 100 grams, i.e., a few centimeters to 1 meter in diameter). Because this observation was also recorded on the REFORME network (meteor observers) at the same time (within one minute) by several observers, the meteoritic origin of the phenomenon is beyond doubt. REFORME recorded the magnitude as -10, making it an exceptional object. To see the video on the internet: (bolide of November 26, 2011).

summary: Observation of the horizontal movement of four white balls: probable observation of Thai lanterns.
description: On November 26, 2011, at 9:05 PM, a witness observed four luminous orbs moving silently for five minutes. The observation matches the characteristics of Thai lanterns: a group of luminous points, moving with the wind (from the southwest), and lasting for a few minutes. The time and day (Saturday evening) are quite common for this type of festive event. It should be noted, however, that the witness described white lights: even white lanterns typically emit a yellow-orange light. This case is classified as "B": probable Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of the rapid movement of a spherical and white object in the clear sky: lack of information.
description: On November 20, 2011, at 3:20 PM, a witness observed a white, spherical object moving rapidly in the clear sky, which appeared to be "heading towards a passenger plane." The witness observed the object until it disappeared over the horizon two to three minutes later. No other reports were received. The radar data requested from air traffic control only mentions the passenger planes reported by the witness. We investigated whether the witness might have observed a strong Iridium satellite flare, which is sometimes visible during the day. However, no such phenomenon occurred that afternoon of November 20, 2011, in Ourouer-les-Bourdelins. No other hypothesis, which is usually a source of confusion, seems to correspond to the observation. Due to the lack of strangeness and consistency of the UFO's trajectory, this sighting case cannot be concluded other than in "C" due to the lack of independent testimonies and cross-checks.

summary: Observation of the slow movement of a multi-colored point of light in the sky: an astronomical misidentification as Sirius
description: On the night of Sunday, November 20, 2011, around 4:00 AM, a young scout in a community hall was intrigued by a multicolored point of light he observed through a window. He noticed the point moving slowly and then stopping. The child heard no unusual noises during his approximately twenty-minute observation. An investigator was sent to verify the sighting directions at the location. The observed direction corresponded to the position of the very bright star Sirius. However, the sighting did not exactly match the appearance of a fixed star. But given the context of the scene (a 9-year-old child, in the middle of his sleep, in an unfamiliar location), this relative inconsistency is not surprising. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable sighting of Sirius.

summary: Probable sighting of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: A witness reported an observation made on November 19, 2011, at 10:08 PM above their home. Several bright yellow-orange lights moved along a straight SE-NW trajectory. No noise was heard during the observation. The lights disappeared as they gained altitude and at very high speed. The witness's description immediately suggested Thai lanterns. The wind direction indicated by the weather forecast (SE-NW) is consistent with the observation. The time and day (a Saturday evening) are also typical indicators of lantern lechers. No investigation was conducted to determine the possible lecher location (wedding, party).

summary: Observation of the movement of a luminous orange ball: probable passage of a Thai lantern.
description: witness observed a luminous orange ball flying at low altitude from north to south in the southern suburbs of Thionville. The description and movement with the wind (see weather report) perfectly matched the appearance of a Thai lantern. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable Thai lantern.

summary: Observation of a sort of blue rainbow followed by a large orange wheel of significant diameter, instantaneous disappearance: lack of information.
description: On Wednesday, November 9, 2011, at 9:05 PM, several people in a car were intrigued by a brief glimpse of a blue phenomenon (described as a flash, a lightning bolt, a semicircle). Upon arriving home and exiting the vehicle, one of the passengers observed another unusual phenomenon in the sky for 5 to 7 seconds: the witness described a large, stationary orange wheel with a significant diameter. It disappeared instantly. None of the other witnesses saw this second phenomenon at that time. The hypothesis that the Sky Tracker temporarily turned on (perhaps accidentally: the observation lasted only 5 to 10 seconds), and made particularly spectacular by the fog, seemed plausible; however, this hypothesis could not be confirmed by the nightclub manager and was completely refuted by the witness. Given these contradictions, and the brevity of the observation, GEIPAN classifies this case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Sighting of an orange ball the size of a pinhead in the sky: probable sighting of a balloon.
description: On November 6, 2011, around 1 p.m., a witness noticed a sphere in the sky, which he described as being the size of a pinhead, dull orange in color. It appeared to be stationary at a high altitude, though its exact altitude was difficult to determine. The witness briefly looked away and did not see the object again. The observation lasted 10 seconds. No other reports were collected. The hypothesis of an orange balloon floating at approximately 500 meters seems to explain this sighting. Its apparent immobility can be explained, firstly, by the fact that even if the balloon is traveling at the wind speed at ground level (30 km/h), this translates to an apparent angular velocity at 500 m of approximately 1 e/s, a speed difficult for the human eye to perceive against a uniform sky near the zenith. Secondly, the wind at 500 m is not always the same as at ground level. Since helium-filled balloons generally burst quite quickly as they ascend, the sudden disappearance of this balloon is perfectly normal. This case is therefore classified as "B": probable balloon.

summary: Probable sighting of a weather balloon.
description: On October 30, 2011, between 3:10 PM and 3:20 PM, a person spotted a bright, twinkling point in the sky. The object appeared stationary or to be moving very slowly. No noise was heard during this observation. The photos taken by the witness suggest a balloon, similar to those used by Météo-France, which conducts several radiosonde balloon launches daily over metropolitan France. Météo-France launches a weather balloon every day from Bordeaux-Mérignac around 12:00 UTC (2:00 PM local time that day). It is highly probable that the witness observed one of these balloons. This case is classified as "B." Probable cause: weather balloon

summary: Observation of a very bright phenomenon gradually decreasing in intensity: probable sighting of an airplane.
description: On October 26, 2011, at approximately 8:30 PM, a witness observed an extremely bright star in the sky (in the region of the constellation Aquarius). The witness was surprised to see that the brightness gradually decreased until it became a very small point in the sky. The observation suggested the possibility of an aircraft seen head-on, with its landing lights on, at a distance of more than 10 km (which would have obscured the green and red lights), and which had changed direction (see map). This hypothesis, which has not been verified, was presented to the witness, who did not respond. This case is classified as "B" by GEIPAN: probable observation of an aircraft head-on, with its landing lights on.

summary: Long observation of colored light phenomena in a thick cloud; no noise: strange unidentified phenomenon.
description: On October 26, 2011, between 9:30 p.m. and 11:00 p.m., a witness observed several blue, pink, and yellow lights in a single thick cloud above the trees, approximately 200 meters from her house, in a clear sky. These lights flickered on and then off. She woke her friend, who also witnessed the phenomenon but quickly went back to sleep. The witness observed the phenomenon several times over the course of more than an hour from various windows of the house. No unusual noises were heard. Finally, the frightened witness went to bed. No photographs were taken. Neither the witness nor her husband saw any traces on the ground in the following days in the area where the sighting occurred. No other witness statements were collected. None of the hypotheses considered (aircraft, laser, air ionization) were deemed convincing enough to be accepted (see the investigation report). GEIPAN therefore classifies this case as D1 due to its strangeness, and due to the unique nature of the testimony and the absence of recording or trace.

summary: Observations of several bright points in the sky, fixed or moving: lack of information.
description: On the RN12 between Jouars-Ponchartrain (78) and Garches (92), on October 26, 2011, around 7:00 PM, a motorist and his son were intrigued by the presence of stationary or moving lights in the sky. A triangular object was then seen. It seems to us that the initial observation (fixed and aligned lights while the witness was traveling east on the RN12) can easily be explained by a mistaking for airplanes due to the heavy air traffic in the Île-de-France region. However, what followed is more complicated, especially since the description remains vague: a triangular object flashing red and white, then a light with vertical flashing lights that were only white, crossing a portion of the sky in two seconds, do not suggest any usual explanation and constitute the only truly strange elements of this observation, for which we would have appreciated more details. Furthermore, we have received no other similar reports for October 26, 2011, in the Paris region. Rated at low to medium strangeness, this observation is too inconsistent to be definitively concluded. This case is classified as C due to a lack of independent testimonies and corroboration.

summary: Long observation of a luminous phenomenon of colors, static and silent in the sky: probable astronomical observation of Sirius.
description: On October 23, 2011, at approximately 4:45 a.m., a driver and her passenger were intrigued by the presence in the low-altitude sky of a luminous phenomenon of varying colors (blue, red) and seen with unusual shapes. This phenomenon remained stationary, and no noise was heard during the observation, which lasted 45 minutes. The witness then decided to continue driving. Only one witness account of this phenomenon was collected. The strangeness of the observed phenomenon, which remained stationary for over 30 minutes, is not inherent; it is the witness's description (triangles, luminous threads) that makes it seem strange. The evidence is weak since, unfortunately, only one witness was willing to contact us. Because the witness initially recognized a star, then saw details after careful observation, GEIPAN favors this star hypothesis: Sirius, low on the horizon, is a likely candidate. It is often the object of this type of misinterpretation under these observation conditions, which induce strong scintillation (multiple changing colors). However, a notable discrepancy in position is noted between Sirius and the observation direction recorded by the investigator retrospectively, but 18 months later. This case is class B: probable astronomical observation of Sirius.

summary: Observation of successive passages of orange glows at low altitude. Slow and silent movements: lack of information.
description: On October 22, 2011, between 9:20 and 9:30 PM, a witness from their home observed the slow, silent passage of an orange glow at low altitude, which they compared to streetlights. A second glow appeared a few seconds later. The phenomena disappeared into the clouds. The witness dismissed the possibility of Thai lanterns, claiming they had seen them up close before. No other witness statements were collected. The witness's description is entirely consistent with the hypothesis of two Thai lanterns: orange color, movement in the direction of the wind (20 to 30 km/h SE to NW), no noise, and Saturday night. However, the witness, who stated they had seen lanterns from a distance, rejected this hypothesis. GEIPAN, lacking further investigative information, classified the case as "C" (insufficient data to draw a conclusion), while clearly favoring the hypothesis of sky lanterns.

summary: Observation of an atmospheric reentry followed by lights in a field: probable observation of a combine harvester.
description: On October 21, 2011, at 9:05 PM, a motorist on the A10 motorway was intrigued by the passage of a luminous phenomenon in the sky, followed by the presence of luminous circles and a cloud of dust in a field. After the chance sighting of a fireball (meteorite impact) while driving, the witness observed white and flashing lights near the road, above a field, as well as a cloud of dust. The description strongly suggests a combine harvester, probably operating on corn. Agricultural vehicles are required to be equipped with an orange flashing light, which may have been left on even though the machine was not on the road. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable sighting of a combine harvester (see examples of combine harvesters seen at night in photos).

summary: Observation across France of the passage of a luminous phenomenon: probable atmospheric reentry of a meteorite or space debris.
description: Numerous people reported seeing a bright phenomenon in the sky on October 21, 2011, around 8:00 PM. Witnesses were located in various departments across France. The descriptions perfectly matched those of a fireball: a bright light with a green trail, a straight trajectory, and a duration of a few seconds. A fireball is defined as the phenomenon produced by the entry into the upper atmosphere of a large meteorite (weighing more than 100 grams, i.e., a few centimeters to 1 meter in diameter). Since this observation was also recorded on the REFORME network (meteor observers) at the same time (within two minutes) and by several observers in northern France, the reality of the phenomenon is beyond doubt. REFORME recorded the magnitude as -6, which classifies it as an average object. It could also have been an atmospheric reentry of uncatalogued space debris. This case is class "B": probable meteorite re-entry or space debris.

summary: Observation of the slow movement OE of a bright white point in the sky and sudden disappearance: probable observation of the passage of the ISS disappearing into the shadow of the earth.
description: On October 20, 2011, at approximately 9:10 PM, an amateur astronomer observed the slow west-to-east movement of a bright point of light. This observation, of low oddity and good consistency, describes a particularly bright point of light moving from west to east, rising towards the celestial vault, and disappearing within a few seconds. This corresponds perfectly to the appearance of the ISS disappearing into the Earth's shadow. A slight discrepancy is noted between the disappearance time (9:03 PM) provided by the simulator and the observation time (9:10 PM), and the maximum elevation is lower than the witness's reading (50th versus 60th/70th). The ISS orbit reports vary considerably from day to day during this period, probably due to maneuvers; obtaining a highly accurate orbit report is very difficult in these situations. This case is class B: probable observation of the International Space Station ISS.

summary: Quick observation of the SW movement of three bright white points in the sky: lack of information.
description: On the evening of Monday, October 17, 2011, at approximately 8:40 PM, the witness was standing in front of his house when he saw a group of three bright white lights, seemingly five times the size of stars, moving across the sky from south to west. The three lights moved in a triangular formation, appearing to separate before regrouping and disappearing over the western horizon. The speed of the entire display was comparable to that of shooting stars, and the observation lasted less than 5 seconds. Of good consistency and low to moderate strangeness, this observation suggests two fairly frequent phenomena: thae lanterns, but the observation period is quite short (unless the witness misjudged the duration), or atmospheric reentry (bolide, meteorite fall), more consistent with the observation time, but the multiplicity of objects is rare. Lacking further investigation to determine which of the two hypotheses is correct, this case is provisionally classified as C.

summary: motorist observed an orange ball moving in the sky: probably a Thai lantern.
description: On October 10, 2011, at approximately 6:20 a.m., a motorist spotted an orange sphere moving in the sky. The witness photographed the luminous phenomenon, which alternately followed an ascending and descending trajectory. No noise was heard during the observation. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. After receiving information about Thai lanterns (videos, photos, articles), the witness lent credence to this hypothesis. Even though the early hour is unusual for this type of observation, this probability was also accepted by GEIPAN (the French National Center for Experimental and Astronomical Research). The weather conditions (very light, unstable winds) were consistent with the observation. This case is classified as "B," indicating a probable sighting of a Thai lantern.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of a group of luminous objects in the sky: lack of information.
description: On October 7, 2011, at approximately 10:15 PM, a witness observed a luminous phenomenon in the sky for 15 seconds. A group of three pale white, triangular objects, arranged in a triangle, moved northeast/southwest. A fourth object, separate from the group, was further west, moving at the same speed and in the same direction. The entire group moved silently beneath the clouds present that evening and eventually disappeared into the clouds. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. The witness's description of four luminous points moving slowly in a straight line suggests Thai lanterns. However, the triangular shape and the perpendicular movement to the wind (according to data from Nantes and Saint-Nazaire provided by Météociel) do not confirm this hypothesis; the witness also did not recognize these lanterns. The aircraft hypothesis is also quite unsuitable: the triangular shape of the lights, the silence. Given these factors, GEIPAN classifies this case as "C": unidentifiable due to lack of data.

summary: Observations by several people of the fall of a grey, tubular-shaped object: probable observation of a tubular thermal balloon.
description: On October 1, 2011, around 5:00 PM, four people sitting in the garden of a house in Carrières-sous-Poissy (78) were frightened by the sight of an oval-shaped object falling rapidly from the sky. Shaped like a capsule, the object appeared horizontal, oscillated, and rotated. It was gray and metallic in appearance. Fearing they would be crushed, the witnesses left the garden and fled in their car. They alerted passersby who saw nothing, as the sky was obscured by trees. The witnesses stopped near a stadium a few hundred meters away, looked behind them, but could no longer see anything. Another person encountered by the main witness reported seeing the object heading towards Triel-sur-Seine (78) in a north-northwest direction. The witnesses, quite intrigued, returned home. Given that the object moved with the wind (see investigation report), the hypothesis of a lighter-than-air balloon is favored. The tubular shape is known to some enthusiasts. The swirling, wind-driven movement is consistent with this hypothesis. The gray plastic film used for these balloons gives a metallic appearance once inflated and exposed to sunlight. The size and distance of the object could not be precisely estimated by the witnesses, who had never seen this type of object before. This modest size (around 3 meters) also explains why so few witnesses noticed it. GEIPAN classifies this case as B: probable observation of a tubular thermal balloon.

summary: Observation of the rapid movement of a bright circular object in the sky: lack of information.
description: On October 1, 2011, at 8:33 PM, a witness observed a luminous circular object silently passing across the sky for 30 seconds. The direction of the observed movement, from East-Southeast to West-Northwest, is consistent with the wind direction. However, the description of the UFO, a perfect brownish disc with a slightly luminous or lighter circle in its center, does not correspond to any commonly observed aerostats (Thai lanterns or balloons). Finally, the relative speed of the movement (30 seconds of observation before the UFO was obscured by buildings) suggests that the object was moving faster than the wind (under similar conditions, Thai lantern sightings last at least a minute). Given the unusual nature of the observed object and its relatively good consistency, this observation is provisionally classified as Class C due to a lack of corroborating evidence. This type of observation leaves few leads to investigate; an on-site investigation would yield little information.

summary: Observations of a probable passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On October 1, 2011, at approximately 10:30 PM, witnesses observed several luminous yellow-orange orbs moving silently across the sky. One of the witnesses recorded a video with their cell phone. After analyzing the video, it became clear that the lights were moving slightly relative to one another. The weather forecast for the day indicated a very light wind whose direction was changing from hour to hour; it was not possible to verify if the movement was consistent with the wind. The overall appearance of the video, the witnesses' accounts, and the time and date (Saturday evening) support the hypothesis of Thai lanterns. No search was conducted for the possible launch site, as there are too many possibilities in the suburban area. This case is therefore classified as "B": probable passage of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of luminous phenomena in the sky: lack of information.
description: On September 30, 2011, at approximately 10:00 PM, a witness observed a stationary point of light quite low on the horizon. Forty-five minutes later, the witness saw the phenomenon begin to move and travel northward, crossing half the sky in about a minute. The first part of the observation, concerning a stationary object, could be consistent with the star Arcturus in the constellation Boötes. The second part, in which the flashing white and red point of light begins to move northward and disappears in about a minute, is more difficult to explain. The hypothesis of an astronomical misinterpretation has been ruled out, and mistaking it for a passenger plane is unlikely given its characteristic lights, leaving the possibility of an unlisted (military) satellite, which we have not been able to verify. Of low strangeness and good consistency, this observation case can be classified as B, indicating a probable misidentification with the star Arcturus for the first part, and C for the second observation. Overall, this case is classified as C due to a lack of information and corroboration.

summary: Observation of three bright points in the sky: lack of information.
description: On September 28, 2011, at approximately 8:25 PM, a driver and his passenger briefly observed several lights in the sky. This observation, of moderate strangeness and consistency (precise testimony, two non-independent witnesses), only allows for the hypothesis of luminous balloons, but this hypothesis could not be supported by any further information (see investigation report). GEIPAN classifies this case as C due to a lack of corroborating evidence.

summary: Observation of the movement of a luminous phenomenon in the sky: lack of information.
description: On September 27, 2011, at 10:10 PM, a witness observed a fixed point of light from his terrace, pointing eastward. Ten minutes later, he was intrigued by a light that appeared at the treetops and rose into the sky at an oblique angle and a steady speed. Of low strangeness and moderate to weak consistency, this observation has not found a definitive explanation among the usual hypotheses, although some of these hypotheses are compatible. This case is classified as Class C due to a lack of information to support the hypotheses considered.

summary: Observation in the sky of the movement of a large, flat, orange object near a helicopter: lack of information.
description: On December 4, 2011, GEIPAN received a Terrestrial Questionnaire (QT) by email from a witness to an observation of an orange, saucer-shaped light on the night of Saturday, September 24, to Sunday, September 25, 2011. As the witness contacted us nearly four months after the event, filing the testimony with the Gendarmerie was no longer possible. The observation lasted between 10 and 15 minutes and took place in the presence of another witness initially, then three other people who were able to see the end of the observation as the object moved away. None of the other witnesses, however, submitted a statement to GEIPAN. Although the lantern hypothesis is favored, the usual evidence supporting this hypothesis is insufficient: the wind direction is imprecise, and the description of the distance leaves its interpretation uncertain. The helicopter, likely taking off from the hospital, merely drew the witness's attention skyward. Unusual and lacking in consistency (only one witness, imprecise testimony), this case is classified as C due to a lack of information or other testimonies.

summary: Observation of the horizontal movement of a luminous fluorescent green and red phenomenon: probable observation of the passage of a bolide.
description: On September 24, 2011, at 3:35 a.m., a Parisian taxi driver observed from his vehicle the silent, horizontal movement of a fluorescent green object with a red line. The object crossed his field of vision and quickly disappeared. No other reports of this phenomenon were collected. Of good consistency and of low to moderate strangeness, this observation has the characteristics of a bolide (atmospheric entry of a meteoroid): a luminous green phenomenon with a trail, moving linearly over a few seconds. Due to the fact that the phenomenon was likely recorded by only one of the cameras in the BOAM network (meteoroid observer network), whereas at least two would have been needed, a firm and definitive conclusion is not strictly possible. This case is classified as Class B: probable observation of a bolide (atmospheric entry of a meteoroid).

summary: Observation of the passage of an orange luminous phenomenon which the witness takes for a plane in flames: lack of information.
description: On Saturday, September 17, 2011, around 11 p.m., a witness on his balcony was intrigued by the passage of an object he initially mistook for a burning airplane heading towards Bordeaux-Mérignac Airport (from south to north), at an altitude of approximately 40 degrees. The observation lasted about 1 minute and 15 seconds. This case of observing red lights moving silently resembles several known phenomena, but certain characteristics of the observation do not fit: atmospheric reentry of a satellite or space debris does not account for the momentary stop and change of trajectory observed; astronomical or atmospheric hypotheses also do not seem to apply. Although the described colors (red, orange, yellow) evoke flames, and the time and day are consistent with a festive event, the hypothesis of a Thae lantern (flying lantern) is unsuitable: its shape is inappropriate, its direction changes, and its appearance changes. The hypothesis of a motorized and illuminated aerostat or dirigible for festive or commercial purposes seems compatible with the observation and cannot be entirely ruled out, given that the sighting occurred on a Saturday evening. However, we have not found any record of such an event. This flimsy case (only one witness), and moderately strange, is classified as category C due to a lack of independent testimonies and corroboration.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon: astronomical observation of Acturus.
description: On September 13, 2011, at 11:15 PM, the gendarmerie was contacted by people who had spotted an unidentified flying object. The gendarmerie went to the scene, and the witnesses reported seeing an ovoid object in the sky with three distinct lights, initially stationary and then moving slowly northward. The witness himself offered an explanation, stating that he had seen the star Mira Ceti (in the constellation Cetus). However, this star was visible to the east at that time, while the witness indicated that he had observed it to the west, in the direction of Rosans. Furthermore, the witness reported seeing the star disappear: a star visible to the east rises in the sky during the night. (See the document "Eastern Celestial Chart"). The observed star was therefore Arcturus, a very bright star (Magnitude 0), which sets around 11:30 PM in the West, moving towards the North. Like all bright stars, its color turns orange at sunset, and it twinkles particularly brightly. (See the document "Western Star Chart"). This case is Class A: identified.

summary: Probable sightings of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On Saturday, December 10, 2011, at approximately 11:45 PM, several people observed lights in the sky that intrigued them. The witnesses' reports were entirely consistent with the observation of Thai lanterns: objects flying with the wind, yellow-orange in color, with a brighter center. The time and day (near midnight on a Saturday night) are typical for this type of phenomenon. Identifying the person who licked these lanterns would allow this case to be classified as "A". However, without this information, GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable observation of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observations of the rapid and silent passage of a luminous phenomenon in the sky: probable observation of an atmospheric reentry.
description: On September 9, 2011, at approximately 10:10 PM, several people in the same neighborhood of Montauban observed a luminous phenomenon moving rapidly and silently from south to north in the sky. Two independent eyewitness accounts have reached us: during the brief observation (lasting from 5 to 30 seconds), the observed phenomenon appeared to have the shape of a "water droplet" or a "white bean," moving quickly and illuminating nothing outside the object itself. No sound was heard during the observation of the object, which gradually decreased in size. This phenomenon, observed by two independent witnesses, described a luminous object in flight moving from south to north for a duration of 7 to 30 seconds. The investigation initially focused on Thai lanterns, or on a possible connection to the "Fête des 400 Coups" (Festival of 400 Blows) which was taking place that day in Montauban. The two witnesses completely refuted these hypotheses. Further analysis suggested the observation was more likely due to the atmospheric reentry of a meteor or satellite debris. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable observation of a bolide.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of a dozen flying objects: likely Thai lanterns
description: On September 3, 2011, at approximately 10:50 PM, a witness observed, from their balcony overlooking the Seine, a formation of about a dozen spheres arranged in a pyramid. This formation moved silently in the opposite direction to the usual flight paths of planes descending towards Orly Airport. As the witness grabbed their camera, some of the objects disappeared, leaving only two, which quickly vanished as they rose towards a large cloud. This observation is quite typical of Thai lantern releases. The red color of the envelope, the group movement, the upward movement and/or movement with the wind (a light easterly wind that evening), the disappearance (extinction) after a few minutes, and the day and time (Saturday evening) of the observation all support this hypothesis. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable observation of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of several orange light points in the sky: observation of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On Saturday, September 3, 2011, at approximately 11:15 or 11:30 PM, a witness and his wife observed several orange lights moving silently in the sky above the southwest horizon. During the approximately two-minute observation, several other orange lights appeared with the same flight characteristics. Due to a particularly detailed questionnaire, this observation, of low strangeness and very good consistency, most likely corresponds to the sighting of several Thae lanterns in the process of extinction. The witness, informed of this hypothesis, viewed photos and videos of lanterns and perfectly recognized this object. This case is classified as Class A: observation of Thae lanterns.

summary: Observation of the rapid and silent passage of three yellowish lights in the sky: probable observation of the movement of Thai lanterns.
description: A witness reported an observation made on September 1, 2011, at 10:35 PM: while on his terrace, he observed the rapid and silent east-west passage of three yellowish lights. These lights disappeared behind a cloud. The observation of these yellowish points crossing the sky in the direction of the wind (see Lorraine weather forecast) is entirely consistent with the observation of Thai lanterns, launched east of Bar-le-Duc (perhaps near the stadium). GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable observation of Thai lanterns.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of orange luminous phenomena
description: On August 28, 2011, at approximately 12:35 a.m., a motorist and his wife observed a silent, NNW-E movement of orange dots in the sky. The witnesses later distinguished seven triangles that appeared equilateral, each with a rounded shape inside one of its vertices. The observation lasted about a minute before the phenomenon disappeared, rapidly diminishing in size due east. The description of the phenomenon (number of objects, color, speed) perfectly matches that of Thai lanterns. The date and time (Saturday night/Sunday morning), along with the westerly wind direction, reinforce this hypothesis.

summary: Recent testimony of an old observation of a light grey cylindrical object seen in orange weather: lack of information.
description: Two people were watching the landscape and lightning of a dry thunderstorm from their homes. They were intrigued by the presence of a light gray cylindrical object between the clouds and the rooftops. The stationary object suddenly disappeared. The observation lasted less than a minute. This case of observation is poorly documented, the observation was brief, and it was reported late. Two hypotheses can be considered: a cylindrical balloon that suddenly burst, or a complex atmospheric phenomenon linked to the storm (plasma). GEIPAN cannot confirm either of these hypotheses. Due to a lack of information, GEIPAN classifies it as case "C," a case not considered particularly unusual.

summary: Presence of lights on photograph without direct visual contact during shooting: internal reflections in the camera lens.
description: witness noticed four lights in photographs that went unnoticed when the pictures were taken. These four bright spots in the sky are artifacts from streetlights, caused by internal reflections within the camera lens. This is evidenced by the fact that the lines connecting each of the first four streetlights from the left to the four lights in the sky from the right intersect at precisely the same point. The other streetlights do not produce artifacts because they are further from the optical center.

summary: Observations of the movement of luminous phenomena in the sky on a downward trajectory: lack of information.
description: On August 26, 2011, around 6:00 a.m., a witness and his wife were intrigued by the slow movement of a luminous phenomenon descending across the sky. The characteristics of this observation and its two-minute duration suggest the possibility of an atmospheric reentry of a satellite or space debris. Such a phenomenon should, however, have been observed by a large number of witnesses spread over a wide area (northern France, Belgium, the Netherlands), yet we found no record of it on that date, suggesting a very localized event. The movement, consistent with wind, could suggest a group of aerostats, but with varying shapes, colors, and light intensities, making it difficult to identify the exact type of passive aircraft. Furthermore, not all the observed objects appear to have the same speed or follow the same trajectory, particularly the last point of light crossing the witness's field of vision at a speed far exceeding all the others. Finally, the hypothesis of a civilian or military air exercise taking place directly above BA112, approximately forty kilometers northeast of the observation site (and therefore at 20° latitude from the observation direction), cannot be ruled out, but we were unable to verify it. This observation case presents a certain strangeness at first glance, but suffers from a lack of precision preventing any firm conclusion. A field investigation aimed at better assessing the trajectories and orientations would provide more information. This case is provisionally classified as Class C, pending further information.

summary: Observation of the movement of two or three orange lights in the sky: lack of information.
description: On March 1, 2012, GEIPAN received a terrestrial questionnaire (QT) by email from a witness to an observation of several lights on the evening of Thursday, August 25, 2011, a little over five months after the event. These different lights merged into a single, fixed point of light before disappearing. Of moderate strangeness and good consistency, this observation leaves two hypotheses, both possible but unlikely: model aircraft and Thai lanterns (see investigation report). An on-site investigation could potentially identify other witnesses to the phenomenon. This case is provisionally classified as Class C pending further simultaneous reports.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of a flying machine.
description: On Wednesday, August 24, 2011, at approximately 3:32 a.m., a witness observed a flying object silently passing by from their home. The triangular shape and the light beneath the object surprised the witness. The phenomenon was quickly obscured by the urban landscape. After verifying with civil aviation authorities and the CNOA (National Air Navigation Center) that there was no radar trace, GEIPAN (French Group for the Study of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena) interviewed the witness about the sighting. The interview confirmed the credibility of the testimony but found no new evidence or information. Due to the lack of a convincing hypothesis, GEIPAN classified this case as D1: Unidentified Phenomenon of weak consistency: only one witness, no recorded trace.

summary: Observation of luminous phenomena in the sky and the passage of a dark mass and a beam of light towards the ground.
description: Two people observed luminous phenomena in the sky from their homes on several dates, including the movement of a dark mass and a beam of light illuminating the ground. No other reports of these phenomena for the dates indicated have been collected. Some of the luminous phenomena can be explained by the passage of airplanes and satellites, and especially by the observation of the star Arcturus, which was exhibiting strong twinkling on those days; this case could be classified as fully explained (Class A). However, the white light illuminating the ground with a beam, as well as the dark object and the white and mauve light directed towards the witness, remain unexplained for the time being, with too little concrete evidence to allow for further investigation.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon that disappears and then reappears in the sky: probable aircraft sighting.
description: After a scuba dive at 10:00 AM on August 20, 2011, at the "Punta d'Arco" site near Bastia, witnesses were surprised to observe a stationary luminous phenomenon in the sky for five minutes. It then suddenly disappeared and reappeared with a different shape, accompanied by a small light to its right. The phenomenon then vanished completely. The investigation revealed that there was heavy air traffic over the observed area that day. The witnesses, who were facing the sun, likely saw several aircraft pass by in succession, which would only have been visible for the time it took for them to reflect the sun, or for the duration of their landing lights being directed towards them. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": probable aircraft sighting.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon: rapid movement of a "star". Lack of information.
description: On August 19, 2011, during an evening walk (between 10:45 p.m. and 11:00 p.m.), a witness was intrigued by a "very large star": initially stationary, it rapidly rose to the zenith before disappearing. No unusual noise was heard during the observation, which lasted approximately 10 seconds. A very bright point in the night sky, at the beginning of the night, which suddenly disappeared, suggested a satellite entering the Earth's shadow. The International Space Station (ISS) was visible that evening. The lack of precision in the witness's account makes it impossible to verify precisely that it was indeed the ISS that was seen. The perception of the disappearance at the zenith is probably an optical illusion, common with the sudden disappearance of bright points of light. GEIPAN classifies this case as "C": insufficient information for a precise investigation.

summary: Observation of the slow movement of a bright point in the sky: probable observation of an aircraft in the landing phase.
description: On August 11, 2011, around 11:00 PM, a witness observed a point of light moving slowly in a straight line from his home. He filmed the phenomenon before it disappeared behind some trees. This witness had already observed the same phenomenon in June 2011. Of low oddity and consistent quality, this observation appears to be a case of mistaken identity involving an aircraft on landing. However, the relative distance of the observation point from the main airports of the Île-de-France region, which were most likely approaching from the east that evening, prevents us from classifying it as Class A. This case is therefore classified as Class B.

summary: Observation of the passage of a point of light in the sky and the particular zig-zag movement: observation of the passage of a satellite and autokinetic illusion.
description: On August 4, 2011, at 10:59 PM, a witness observed a bright point of light passing across the sky. He was intrigued by the object's zigzag movements and variations in intensity. No noise was heard during the observation. The object disappeared from the witness's field of vision. The witness's description: a bright white point of light crossing the sky from south to north suggests the passage of a satellite. On this trajectory, and at the time in question, the passage of the satellite IGS1B, of magnitude 2 (like Polaris), was recorded. Its brightness changes during the passage, depending on its exposure to the sun. Of course, viewed from the ground, a satellite moves in a strictly straight line (or a slightly curved one), which does not correspond to the witness's account. The zigzags described by the witness may be due to an optical illusion of physiological origin called autokinetic illusion, which occurs when the eye follows a point of light against a completely black background. See pages 26 and 30 of the document: /typo3conf/ext/dam_frontend/pushfile.php?docID=9932. This case is class B: probable observation of a satellite's passage with autokinetic illusion.

summary: Observations of the movement of several phenomena in the sky: lack of information.
description: witness observed two distinct phenomena in the Bordeaux sky on two separate occasions. The first was on the evening of August 3, 2011, starting at 9:00 PM, and the second was in the night of August 6-7, 2011, at 3:15 AM. The second observation, which corresponds in every respect to a misidentification of Thai lanterns, will not be discussed in this report. Regarding the first observation, while the movement of the UFO seems consistent with the wind (subject to correct interpretation of its positions and directions), its appearance is unremarkable. A hot air balloon, however unusual, should have been recognizable, particularly at sunset and in the absence of clouds. Our best hypothesis remains the possible observation of a lenticular cloud, a rare and therefore surprising phenomenon. But again, sunset should have revealed its nature, unless the horizon was obscured by clouds. Of medium strangeness, but with too little consistency in its current state, this case is provisionally class C pending new elements.

summary: Observation of the atmospheric reentry of a bolide.
description: On Tuesday, August 2, 2011, between 3:27 and 3:35 a.m., several dozen witnesses observed a sky suddenly brightening as if it were daylight, followed by an object, often described as green/blue, that passed by for 4 to 5 seconds. Some of them also heard one or two explosions a few seconds after the phenomenon passed. A few reported fragmentation. The fifty or so witnesses located across a large southern region (Ariège, Aveyron, Aude, Gironde, Haute-Garonne, Tarn, and Tarn-et-Garonne) who contacted GEIPAN provided precise details about this observation. The preliminary data thus collected indicate a north-south trajectory, with a slight east-west offset. The fireball appears to have ended its trajectory in a triangular area encompassing Andorra, Carcassonne, and Perpignan. (See the GEIPAN website for the news item "A fireball on August 2nd in the sky over southern France" and the map in .kmz format). Scientists from the IMCCE (Institute of Celestial Mechanics and Ephemeris Calculation) identified this phenomenon as a fireball. See http://www.reforme-meteor.net and the GEIPAN summary report.

summary: Observation during a video recording of a phenomenon in the sky.
description: On August 2, 2011, while filming the landscape, a person was startled to see an unidentified object flash past their lens very quickly. No sound was heard. They handed over their photographs to the police. The video clearly shows an insect crossing the field of vision in the last two seconds. The very fleeting phenomenon that appears at the 5-second mark is very likely also a yellow insect, passing even closer to the lens than the one at the end of the video.

summary: Observation of a stationary luminous phenomenon in the sky: lack of information.
description: On August 2, 2011, at approximately 8:15 PM, a driver and her son observed a bright, stationary white light in the sky above the rooftops of downtown Langon. Continuing on their way, the witnesses lost sight of the phenomenon. Only the driver's account is recorded. Due to the geometry of the observation (observed opposite the sun, shortly before sunset), several sources compatible with the characteristics of this sighting can be considered: a reflection of the sun on the fuselage of a distant aircraft, a reflection on a weather balloon launched from Bordeaux-Mérignac, a reflection on a child's balloon (a metallic balloon) launched from Langon, or even a temporary reflection on a satellite. In any case, we were unable to definitively identify the source of this possible misinterpretation. Slightly unusual and of moderate consistency, this case cannot be definitively concluded at this stage, but is most likely a reflection of the sun on an ordinary flying object. This case is class C due to a lack of independent testimony and corroboration.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon in the sky: aircraft approaching Cannes airport.
description: On August 1, 2011, at approximately 12:25 PM, a driver and his passenger noticed a bright object in the sky. The object appeared stationary and then suddenly disappeared. The phenomenon was observed for 4 to 5 seconds. Sightings of temporary bright spots in broad daylight are generally explained by flashes from Iridium satellites or by approaching aircraft seen head-on. In this case, Air Navigation Services indicated a Falcon 900 approaching Cannes Airport precisely where the witness saw it and at the specified time. It is possible that the observed light, in addition to the aircraft's searchlight, was also a reflection of the sun on the aircraft. When the aircraft banked to align with the runway centerline, the witness was no longer directly in line with the searchlights, and the light appeared to vanish. When a point of light disappears from the sky (as is the case with satellites passing into the Earth's shadow), witnesses often interpret its disappearance as a sudden departure. Because the aircraft responsible for the luminous phenomenon has been identified, this case is classified as "A": perfectly identified.

summary: Observation of a probable atmospheric reentry.
description: witness reported observing a very rapid passage of a white, oval-shaped object across the sky on July 31, 2011, at approximately 7:30 PM. It moved silently and disappeared quickly over the horizon. The object's speed and brightness suggest the re-entry of a meteoroid or space debris into the atmosphere. The date of the observation coincides with the period of numerous meteor showers, and the direction of the trajectory is consistent with a Perseid meteor shower. The report has been forwarded to meteorite specialists (IMCCE and the National Museum of Natural History) for their information.

summary: Observations of the silent passage of 7 red balls in the sky.
description: At 11:30 PM, several people observed from their terraces overlooking the town of Limoux the successive appearance of several red orbs in the sky, a few minutes apart. No sound was heard as these seven orbs slowly passed under the clouds. No other accounts of this phenomenon were collected. The description of the phenomenon perfectly matches that of Thai lanterns. The date and time (Saturday late evening), and the wind direction (from west to east), which allowed the lanterns launched near Limoux to be carried towards the observer, all reinforce this hypothesis. Note: the witness observed that the clouds were coming from the east; if these were high-altitude clouds, this is consistent with a west-east wind at ground level.

summary: Observations of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On July 23, 2011, at approximately 11:30 PM, two people observed a group of orange lights moving across the sky. They gradually disappeared towards the horizon. The witnesses' account, the video, the photos (particularly DSC03604.JPG), and the wind direction (from the NW) are entirely consistent with the observation of Thai lanterns, likely released in the Compiègne forest. The day and time (a Saturday evening) are also typical for a lantern release following a festival. Because the photo clearly shows the lantern, this case is classified as "A".

summary: Observation of the successive movements of two red-orange luminous phenomena in the sky: probable observation of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On July 22, 2011, starting at 10:15 PM, a witness observed, at 10-minute intervals, the silent movement of luminous red-orange objects across the sky. The objects disappeared in a south-southeast direction. Each observation lasted 3 minutes. Due to the single witness, this case is of low strangeness and medium to low consistency, exhibiting all the characteristics of a mistaken observation of Thai lanterns. This case is classified as Class B, a Thai lantern sighting.

summary: Observation of the appearance and disappearance of several orange spheres with flashes of white light: probable observation of aircraft close to landing.
description: On July 18, 2011, at approximately 9:15 PM, a witness was intrigued by the presence of several luminous orange orbs and white flashes of light above a hill in the Tanneron massif. The witness quickly noticed the disappearance of some of the orbs followed by the sudden appearance of others. No noise was heard during the observation. The witness took numerous photographs from their home. While of low oddity and good consistency, this observation, at least in its photographic form, is a clear case of mistaken identity involving aircraft circulating around Nice Airport, which were unusually configured that evening due to strong westerly winds. Other details mentioned by the witness also suggest civilian aircraft, although the imprecision of the testimony prevents us from confirming this. This case is classified as Class B: probable observation of aircraft nearing landing.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of an orange glow: probable observation of a Thai lantern.
description: witness reported an observation made with his wife: on July 14, 2011, at 11:49 PM, they observed a bright orange light silently passing across the sky. The object moved at a constant speed along a straight trajectory. A video was recorded with a cell phone during the last 43 seconds the object was visible. (The witness uploaded their video to the internet. The description matches the characteristics of a Thai lantern: size, light, movement, date, and time. However, the origin of the lecher was not investigated, and the case is classified as Class B. The police report, received on November 4, 2011, suggests that the phenomenon could be a flying wing whose brightness is explained by the presence of diodes connected to a battery.)

summary: Filmed observation of the passage of Thai lanterns.
description: On Sunday, July 10, 2011, between 12:30 and 12:45 a.m., several people observed about ten bright orange lights passing across the sky, forming a large cluster. The main witness reacted quickly, filming the sighting with his camera while simultaneously calling the police. On Friday, July 15, 2011, at 11:22 p.m., the witness reported another sighting of a similar phenomenon. The video of the first sighting, which the witness provided to the police, is typical of a sighting of Thai lanterns. GEIPAN (the French National Geographic Institute) highlights the exemplary investigation conducted by the police, which concluded that Thai lanterns were indeed present. Even though formal proof was not provided, the witness supported the conclusion, and GEIPAN fully endorsed it.

summary: Observations of an object crossing the sky on a downward trajectory towards the sea. Presence of a visible trail behind this sphere.
description: Several people from the Isle of Pines (New Caledonia) reported what they observed on July 10, 2011, at around 5:30 PM: a round object crossed the sky diagonally on a downward trajectory toward the sea. Several colors and a trail were noted. No sound was heard. A white flash was seen before the phenomenon completely disappeared. The witnesses most likely observed a bolide, caused by the impact of a meteorite or space debris. The accounts, although varying, are consistent with this phenomenon. As there is no proof of the object's origin, this case is classified as B: probable meteorite impact.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of three luminous balls on a straight trajectory: lack of information.
description: On the morning of Sunday, July 3, 2011, around 8:30 a.m., the witness, who was using his personal computer, decided to go out for a cigarette on the south-southwest facing terrace of his residence. He then noticed three bright white orbs in the sky, also heading south-southwest. Two of them moved closer together, and the three objects together began to move in a straight line from southwest to northwest, without the noise or condensation typical of high-altitude airliners, and with an apparent speed greater than that of such aircraft. The witness interrupted his observation to look for his camcorder, then changed his mind and used his cell phone instead. The phenomenon had disappeared when he returned to the terrace a few moments later, and he was unable to see it again through his west-facing windows. The observation lasted approximately 60 seconds. This case of three luminous orbs crossing a portion of the sky appears to be of moderate strangeness, as they resemble balloons. Since the wind, measured at 7 km/h, is contrary to the observed movement, this hypothesis cannot be confirmed nor definitively ruled out. This case suffers from insufficient evidence at this stage: a single witness statement, no photograph, and uncertainty regarding the wind direction. Without further information to validate or exclude either of these hypotheses, GEIPAN classifies this case as C e.

summary: Observation of the passage of a Thai lantern.
description: On Saturday, July 2, 2011, at approximately 10:30 PM, two people observed the silent passage of an orange spherical object flying in a downward trajectory across the sky. Flames were seen at the base of the object. The sphere quickly disappeared as it ascended. The witness's description corresponds to that of a Thai lantern, and its movement is consistent with the wind that day (a north wind). It is possible that this lantern was licked at the end of the medieval festival that took place that day in Bergues, but GEIPAN was unable to contact the festival organizer to confirm this hypothesis. This case was initially classified as Class B: probable Thai lantern. A new witness contacted GEIPAN in December 2012 to confirm that it was indeed a lantern (see letter and photo IMG 5081), allowing this case to be reclassified as Class A.

summary: Observation in the sky of a cluster of black balls appearing to rotate on itself: lack of information.
description: Recent report (October 1, 2014) of an old observation without a specific date and uncertainty regarding the month. In June or July 2011, at 6:30 PM, a witness observed a cluster of black balls in the sky, with a very blurry appearance. The altitude was quite low (no more than 1000m). The object appeared to rotate. The witness's description of the phenomenon remains entirely consistent with a cluster of balloons, probably released unintentionally. Only the blurry outline might be surprising: a hazy atmosphere or slight glare from backlighting could cause this effect. As the precise date is unknown, GEIPAN was unable to conduct the appropriate investigations for this type of phenomenon (verification of movement relative to local wind, search for the lechers or other witnesses). Due to the lack of a precise date, GEIPAN classifies this case as "C" for lack of information.

summary: Probable sighting of a helicopter.
description: While driving their vehicle, a woman and her husband repeatedly observed a moving flying object in the sky. The object's flashing lights and low altitude intrigued them. No unusual noises were heard during the observation. The witness's description is consistent with the appearance of a helicopter in night flight. New helicopters are significantly quieter than conventional ones. The Amiens Gendarmerie Air Section, equipped with these new helicopters, confirmed they were flying in that area that day, but they could no longer specify the exact route taken that night. This case is therefore classified as "B": probable helicopter sighting.

summary: Mistake related to an optical phenomenon: reflection in the lens of the camera.
description: witness sent us a series of photographs in which she discovered "strange elements." No observations were made during the photography. Determined to understand the phenomenon, the witness took another photograph under the same conditions the following day. The same phenomenon appeared again. This case perfectly illustrates a category of technical explanations for seemingly strange photographs: they are reflections within the camera's lens, appearing as "caustics" (a family of surfaces in optics). The shooting conditions for the five photographs taken in Ariège are ideal for the appearance of such optical effects in certain cameras (as it depends on the configuration of the lens elements): a dark landscape with a few bright light sources, creating strong contrast, further enhanced by a long exposure time (between 23 and 35 seconds). The quality of the photos provided allows GEIPAN to open this case in order to concretely illustrate a case of misinterpretation linked to an optical phenomenon essentially due to the use of a digital camera under specific conditions (see the photographic analysis). The case is class A.

summary: Probable sighting of a Thai lantern passing overhead.
description: On the evening of June 27, 2011, two people observed an orange light passing in a straight line directly overhead. No sound was heard during the one-minute observation. The hypothesis of a Thai lantern was favored: its red-orange appearance, shape, and movement according to the wind (north or northwest). GEIPAN classified this case as "B": probable observation of a Thai lantern.

summary: Observations of the silent movement of a luminous phenomenon consisting of three points arranged in a triangle: lack of information.
description: On Sunday, June 26, 2011, at approximately 11:10 PM, a witness was intrigued by the observation of a bright light source moving overhead. As it passed over his house, the witness saw three white/orange points of light arranged in a triangle. No sound was heard during the slow passage and the observation, which lasted four minutes. Another witness present at the scene observed the phenomenon but did not report their observation. In the absence of a validated hypothesis (see the investigation report), this case is classified as C due to a lack of information.

summary: Observation of the rapid and silent movement of lights.
description: witness reported two sightings, one of which occurred around midnight on June 26, 2010. On that date, he observed a bright, white light passing directly over his home. It came from the northwest and quickly disappeared in a southeasterly direction. As it passed over the witness, he noted the presence of three white lights: two in front and one behind, forming a triangular shape. No noise was heard during the sighting. Another witness account of this phenomenon was collected. This sighting exhibited some characteristics of low-flying aircraft, but certain elements were inconsistent (e.g., silence, signaling). GEIPAN (the French National Gendarmerie Intervention Group) searched with civil aviation authorities and the French Air Force for radar traces of aircraft in flight (see document on radar traces): only high-altitude flights were reported. It should be noted that radar does not cover low-altitude flights and that this area is known to the Air Force as it is one of their low-altitude training zones. Given this lack of precise information, GEIPAN classifies this case as "C".

summary: Observation of the silent movement of several luminous points forming a V: lack of information;
description: On June 26, 2011, at 2:30 a.m., a person was stargazing. They were intrigued by a moving point of light, quickly followed by several other points of light (between five and seven). These points moved slowly and silently, aligned in a V-formation, heading west. The description of the orange points in a V-formation suggested sky lanterns. This hypothesis was refuted by the witness, and the possibility of movement with the wind could not be confirmed because the wind was very unstable that night. Since they did not see any stars in the center of the triangle, the witness interpreted the group of points as the perimeter of an object, but they may have been dazzled by the lights. The hypothesis of aircraft flying in formation to the Paris Air Show could not be verified because the investigation was too late. Given these dubious or contradictory elements, GEIPAN classifies this case as "C".

summary: Observation of the movement of a luminous phenomenon that disappears instantaneously: lack of information.
description: On June 24, 2011, at 10:30 PM, a witness was intrigued by the presence of a reddish-purple luminous phenomenon in his neighborhood. He observed this silent phenomenon for about fifteen seconds from his apartment window. The light moved slowly and then disappeared instantly. No other witness statements were collected. The witness's account, as determined by investigators, was unreliable, significantly impacting the credibility of the testimony. The factual information gathered on site did not contribute to a better understanding of the event, nor did it strengthen the witness's testimony. The unique nature of this testimony is surprising in an urban area for such a strange phenomenon. Due to its high degree of strangeness but insufficient consistency, this case of observation is classified as C due to a lack of reliable information.

summary: Probable sighting of an aircraft passing overhead
description: On June 20, 2011, at 11:00 PM, in a field, two people observed a luminous yellow-orange sphere silently passing overhead. After making a turn above the treetops, a triangular shape appeared. Very frightened, they left the area, but one of the witnesses filmed the sighting. The witnesses likely observed an aircraft, as the video shows the object consistent with the appearance of an airplane, with its standard night-time lighting and runway lights illuminated. No investigation was conducted to identify which aircraft was flying over the site.

summary: Observation of the rapid passage of an intense white and flashing light among the stars: lack of information.
description: On August 15, 2011, between 11:30 PM and 11:45 PM, two witnesses were intrigued by the rapid passage of a very intense, flashing white light across the sky. The phenomenon traversed the entire sky. Of moderate strangeness, but lacking sufficient precision (direction, time), this observation suggests phenomena related to sunlight reflecting off an unlisted satellite (or to an atmospheric reentry phenomenon, according to a highly unusual scenario). Since GEIPAN was unable to confirm this hypothesis, the case is classified as C due to a lack of more precise information.

summary: Observation of luminous phenomena at night: indirect observation, via video and photo, of streetlights on the ground.
description: The witness filmed a lunar eclipse on June 15, 2011, and observed three intriguing luminous phenomena. The witness also later noted a fourth phenomenon in the video footage. The videos and photos do not clearly corroborate the witness's account. The first appearance of the phenomenon at 3:48 corresponds to a zoom out, which reveals a point of light in the field of view that was not present in "narrow field" mode. The point of light then appears to "descend" when the zoom level increases again. This is likely a light source close to the ground (e.g., a nearby streetlamp). At 4:02, another point of light appears below the Moon: this is clearly a streetlamp, part of whose base is visible. (The attached ephemerides clearly indicate that the Moon was only 15 degrees above the horizon, therefore quite low, approximately two hours after moonrise.) The witness appears to have observed these phenomena only through the camcorder's viewfinder, and then later during video editing; the zooming in and out operations likely misled him. The photograph showing two luminous "L" shapes corresponds to a long-exposure photograph (due to camera shake) of two bright points, probably the same two sources that captured the video. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": indirect observation, via video and photograph, of streetlights on the ground.

summary: Probable observation of the ISS passing overhead.
description: witness reports that on June 15, 2011, shortly after 11:30 PM, he observed the silent, straight passage of a very bright white sphere across the sky. He cannot explain the observed phenomenon. A passage of the International Space Station (ISS) occurred between 11:08 PM and 11:18 PM, moving from west to east and visible from Aiglemont. Although the witness indicated that he searched online and concluded that the ISS was not visible that evening (NB: these searches may be inaccurate in retrospect), and that the time does not exactly match the one indicated by the witness, the ISS hypothesis is retained, as the trajectory and brightness perfectly correspond to an ISS pass.

summary: Successive observations of the passage of the International Space Station (ISS).
description: Several witnesses observed the regular passage of a bright point along the same trajectory. Considering the times given by the witness, the observation corresponds to the passage of the International Space Station (ISS), to which the ATV2 cargo spacecraft was docked. The witness observed a light moving southward on a southwest-east axis, consistent with the ISS's trajectory. Its magnitude of -3.0 made it a bright object easily visible to the naked eye. The subsequent passage times recorded on the Heavens Above website are slightly off due to the weekly trajectory correction of the station. This case is classified as Class A, like the observation of the International Space Station (ISS).

summary: Observations of the movement of a luminous object and circular trace of flattened grass: lack of information.
